title: Computer networks and security
lead: Lecture explanations, worked lab problems and quiz practice, organized by the concept you need to study.

title: OSI model and encapsulation
lead: A clear map of the OSI layers, their peer relationships, service terms and the way data is wrapped as it moves through a network.

title: Data link framing, errors and flow control
lead: How neighboring devices find frame boundaries, detect corruption, recover missing data, and keep transmissions within receiver capacity.

title: WAN and MAN technologies
lead: Follow the lecture’s historical path from dedicated lines to shared packet services, ATM cells, MPLS labels, and Ethernet First Mile access.

title: LAN, Ethernet and switching
lead: From shared-medium access rules to Ethernet frames, switch learning, VLAN tags, and the two MAC-address labs.

title: Network layer and routing
lead: Routers move packets between networks. The central distinction is between choosing routes for traffic and forwarding each packet using the table that results.

title: IPv4 addressing, subnetting and VLSM
lead: A prefix divides each 32-bit IPv4 address into a network and host part. Once that boundary is clear, you can calculate subnet ranges, check local membership, aggregate routes and allocate mixed-size networks without overlap.

title: IP packets, ARP, ICMP, DHCP and NAT
lead: Follow an IPv4 datagram from its header to a local or routed link, then see how ARP finds the next-hop MAC address, ICMP reports network conditions, DHCP configures a joining host, and NAT tracks replies to translated traffic.

title: IPv6 addressing and transition
lead: IPv6 gives interfaces a 128-bit address and carries packets through a fixed base header that can point to optional extension headers. This page works from address notation and scope to packet handling, coexistence, DNS, and the two-subnet configuration lab.

title: Transport services and connections
lead: How end-to-end transport delivers data to the right process, distinguishes service choices, and handles generic connection and buffer problems.

title: Bluetooth, NFC and ZigBee
lead: Choose a short-range network by matching its topology, protocol support, energy use and application role to what devices actually need to exchange.

title: Security foundations and cryptography
lead: Security starts by deciding what must be protected, identifying who or what could threaten it, and matching each requirement to a control that actually provides it.

title: Public key infrastructure
lead: PKI helps people decide whether a public key really belongs to the identity it names. Certificates, trusted issuers, registration checks, directories, and revocation information work together to support that decision.

title: IPsec and TLS
lead: Trace who terminates IPsec or TLS protection, what each packet mode authenticates or encrypts, and how the lecture’s TLS 1.0-era handshake sets up protected records.

title: Network design
lead: Network design starts with the services an organization needs, then fits the network to its business goals, access rules, existing assets, growth, and traffic.
